claim: "Forty five, fifty days. Sometimes more."
evidence: A bill takes a mean of 37.6 days from invoice date to paid (median 35, p90 54); from the desk date it is 31.3. Only 8.6% of bills land in the 45 to 50 band. What survives is 'sometimes more': 20.3% take over 45 days and 6.4% over 60. Invoices dated to 31 Jan 2026, which have all had time to be paid, give the same picture (mean 38.1).

claim: "Honestly, head office."
evidence: Head office, from receipt to paid (central AP plus the payment run), holds 19.2 of the 37.6 days, about half. The other half is before head office: vendor to desk 6.4, property 7.1, courier 5.0. Inside central AP the biggest piece is the queue before a verifier picks the bill up (8.8 days), not the work (1.6).

claim: "I would say maybe one in five bills."
evidence: 1,441 of 11,000 bills have a query: 13.1%, about 1 in 7.6, not 1 in 5. No invoice month exceeds 14.4%.

claim: "Mostly. Sometimes the property team makes an error in the service entry. But the root is the vendor sending a bad bill."
evidence: By the text of the query the fix sits with the vendor in 42.7% of cases, the largest single side but not a majority. Where the text names no alternative owner only 15.5% are vendor-side; it reaches 51.7% only if every ambiguous query is given to the vendor.

claim: "if we pay a micro or small vendor late, we cannot claim that expense in the year."
evidence: Late payment exists, but its size depends on the clock. Of Micro or Small bills paid, 20.2% took over 45 days from the invoice date, 10.4% from the desk date and 6.0% from property verification. 88 Micro or Small invoices are still unpaid, 43 already past 45 days from the invoice date. The tax consequence itself is not in the data.

claim: "Some vendors registered after they started with us and nobody updated the master."
evidence: 137 of 900 vendors (15.2%) have a blank MSME status, covering 1,620 bills. The blanks are real; that they arose because nobody updated the master is not testable.

claim: "I think the team insists on the physical copy before they book."
evidence: None of the 10,896 posted bills was posted before its packet reached head office (0 exceptions), and 8 queries hold a bill because only a scan has arrived. That fits a practice of waiting for the paper; whether it is required by rule or law is not in the data.

claim: "If the packet is complete, we post it in two days."
evidence: Bills with no query go from AP pick-up to posting in a mean of 1.3 days (median 1, longest 3). From the day the packet arrives it is a median of 9 days, because of the queue.

claim: "Honestly most bills take ten, fifteen minutes to verify."
evidence: The data has dates, not effort. Elapsed pick-to-posting time for bills with no query is a median of 1 day, consistent with it but saying nothing about minutes.

claim: "The problem is never our speed. The problem is what comes to us."
evidence: AP's own verification is 1.6 days of 37.6 (4.2%). But the queue before a verifier starts is 8.8 days, the largest single wait, and one verifier carries 40.3% of the bills. What arrives also matters (13.1% of bills have a query, adding 24.2 days each), so AP is fast once it starts, but 'never our speed' ignores the queue.

claim: "typing is maybe ten percent of our time. Chasing queries is much more. And waiting for packets."
evidence: Typing cannot be measured, only bounded. Active verification is 1.6 days, 12.0% of the days a bill spends in central AP, so typing is at most that. Queries (3.0 days on the overall mean) and the queue (8.8 days) are larger. 'About ten percent' is the right order of magnitude as elapsed time; effort is not in the data.

claim: "Mostly they land Friday, sometimes Monday if the courier is late."
evidence: Every one of the 10,996 packets received is recorded as reaching head office on a Friday (0 on any other day), so 'mostly Friday' is confirmed. No packet is recorded as arriving on a Monday, so 'sometimes Monday' is not in the data.

claim: "But a big share is our own side. Work order, GL, service entry."
evidence: Work order, GL / cost centre and service entry / GRN queries are 679 of 1,441 (47.1%). Property, procurement and head office together are 57.3% on the primary reading and 26.6% where the text gives no alternative owner.

claim: "People put a lot under Other."
evidence: 94 queries (6.5%) are labelled Other: a modest share, though 74 of them carry a text that names a real category.

claim: "A missing challan, a week."
evidence: PF/ESIC challan queries have a median of 22 days to resolve, not a week.

claim: "That can be a month." (work-order amendment)
evidence: Work-order queries have a median of 17 days to resolve, p90 44, longest 154. 22.1% run past 30 days, so a month happens but is not typical.

claim: "In practice when the split is wrong, my verifier stops there."
evidence: The query log holds one row per bill (no bill has two), so a stop-at-the-first-error sequence cannot be seen.

claim: "A vendor in Delhi charges IGST to a property in Delhi, or puts 12 percent where it should be 18."
evidence: IGST-on-intra-state queries (55) and wrong-rate queries (52, all '12 instead of 18') exist. But the extract puts vendor and property in the same state for only 16 of the 55 IGST queries.

claim: "Audit needs the original on file, not in my hand on the day I post."
evidence: A legal question, not a data question (see notes/understanding.md, section 4).

claim: "Fast. Once my team has it, it is out in a day or two. We are not the problem."
evidence: The head's own step is quick: 75.3% are signed within 2 days of verification (median 2, longest 3). But a bill is signed a mean of 7.1 days after the desk logs it (median 6); only 6.7% are signed within 2 days of arrival, and it then takes 5.0 more days to reach head office.

claim: "Honestly, a few days here and there is not the issue. The issue is what happens after."
evidence: The courier is a fixed wait of 2 to 8 days (mean 5.0, 13.2% of the total). It is smaller than central AP (13.2 days) but not 'a few days here and there': property plus courier is 12.1 days.

claim: "Then head office checks everything again and asks us the same questions."
evidence: 366 queries (25.4%) are on items the property checklist already requires (GSTIN, company name, rate, attendance signature, PF/ESIC, gate stamp, service report). The rest are head-office-only checks or problems the property could not know. The data cannot tell a repeated question from a check the property missed.

claim: "The tracker number on the cover was written wrong, so head office had logged it under another vendor."
evidence: No field records which vendor a packet was logged under.

claim: "If the society added two guards in December, the value runs out before March."
evidence: 601 work orders (28.7%) are billed past their approved value, and 560 of them (93.2%) passed it before their validity ended. That it comes from added guards is not testable, and manpower is not special: the share runs 22.7% to 35.3% across categories (security 30.7%, housekeeping 29.2%).

claim: "Courier picks up on Thursday."
evidence: All 10,996 packets received reach head office on a Friday, and the lag from the head's signature is set entirely by the weekday of signing (7 of 7 weekdays have exactly one lag). Signed on a Wednesday it takes 2 days, on a Thursday 8: the Thursday cut-off is real, and a bill signed on a Thursday waits for the following week's courier.

claim: "He tries to do it once or twice a week."
evidence: The head signs within 3 days of verification on every bill (median 2), faster than a once-or-twice-a-week batch would allow. Caution: 28.4% of signature dates fall on a Saturday or Sunday, so the register's signing dates should not be over-read.

claim: "I find out when the service entry fails."
evidence: Nothing records when anyone noticed a work order running out.

claim: "Nobody has time to check SAP for forty work orders every week."
evidence: Work orders per property run from 41 to 77 (median 55).

claim: "The reliever is not in biometric. He signs the gate register."
evidence: All 3 relievers claimed on the bill are absent from the biometric file (0 present) and appear in the gate register (21 gate rows).

claim: "But the reliever's name is spelt differently in two places."
evidence: The attendance files identify people by ID (G101, R-901), not by name, so spelling differences cannot be seen.

claim: "I am doing the attendance for four, five days every month with a highlighter."
evidence: Hours are not in the data. The size of the problem in the February sample: 11 of 17 people claim more days than biometric shows, but only 4 claim more than the gate register shows. A three-way match leaves 4 people to review.

claim: "Once I have all the paper, an amendment is a week. Maybe less. The waiting is for paper."
evidence: The data has no amendment date, so the amendment step cannot be timed. The whole query cycle (which includes the paper) closes within 7 days for 14.0% of work-order queries and within 14 for 41.1%; the median is 17.

claim: "The commercial executive thinks procurement sat on it for five weeks."
evidence: No bill in the data matches the described case (housekeeping, residential, desk 5 Jan 2026, work-order query closed 11 to 14 Feb): 0 matches. The query log also holds one query per bill, whereas the case had three.

claim: "I run a report on the first of every month. Orders ending in the next sixty days."
evidence: 93 of the 107 orders behind an expiry query would have been on a 'next 60 days' list run on the 1st of a month since April 2025, so expiry is predictable. The bills reached the desk a median of 39 days after expiry, and 702 bills are dated after their order's expiry. Whether anyone opens the report is not in the data.

claim: "Two, three a month, maybe." (GL errors)
evidence: There are 6.3 'GL does not match' queries a month, not two or three (17.9 a month if cost-centre queries are included). They are raised on bills, which may follow older orders, so the comparison is approximate.

claim: "Eleven amendment requests in four days. No, twelve" (second week of February)
evidence: Amendment requests are not in the data. Proxy: work-order queries raised 8 to 15 Feb 2026 number 11, against a mean of 3.6 in any 4 days; no February spike.

claim: "I said, sir, these orders were fine in December."
evidence: 244 work orders were already past their approved value by 31 Dec 2025 and 422 by 28 Feb: 178 crossed in January and February. Crossings ran at most 23 a month from April to September and at least 42 a month from October, which fits balances being eaten from the festival months. But 57.8% of those over by February were already over in December.

claim: "Most of them are for a year."
evidence: Median validity is 530 days (about 17 months); 96.7% are at least 300 days but only 6.3% are 330 to 400 days. They are for a year or more, and the extract may show extended dates.

claim: "MSME certificates, if somebody sends one later, it may sit."
evidence: Same evidence as L6.

claim: "Five weeks if everything is fine. Sometimes two months."
evidence: Security bills with no query take a median of 36 days from invoice to paid, about five weeks. Bills with a query take a median of 56.5, and 8.1% of all security bills take over 60 days.

claim: "I registered three years ago. I sent it to procurement by email. Nobody confirmed."
evidence: No security vendor in the data serves six properties (the most is 4), so he cannot be identified. The situation he describes does exist: 10 of 72 security vendors have a blank MSME status.

claim: "Last month they said IGST is wrong. Our office is in Faridabad, the property is in Gurugram, both Haryana."
evidence: 10 of the 55 IGST queries are on bills where vendor and property are both in Haryana, his exact case. For the other 39 the extract says the supply is inter-state.

claim: "Many. Work order finished, so they cannot book."
evidence: Work-order queries are 69 of 306 on security bills (22.5%) and 338 of all 1,441 queries.

claim: "Sometimes they cut the days. I accept it because what can I do."
evidence: In the February sample vendors claim 388 days against 352 in the biometric file and 382 in the gate register. A property that trusts biometric alone would cut 36 days; against the gate register only 6. Whether cuts are made is not in the data.

claim: "Diwali time. October bill." / "Paid in December. Two months."
evidence: 12 of 167 security bills invoiced in October 2025 took over 60 days, so 'two months' happens. But October is no worse than other months (mean 41.4 against 41.0 days).

claim: "Usually I call three, four times for each bill."
evidence: There is no call log. The survey's 'three times per bill' is the only figure.

claim: "Around ninety percent on the main fields." (past OCR pilot)
evidence: A past pilot's accuracy; not in the pack. Our own reader can be measured on the 40 inbox bills.

claim: "It fixed the typing, and typing was not the slow part."
evidence: AP verification with no query open is 1.6 days of 37.6 (4.2%). Removing it entirely would save at most that. The days are in waiting: 81% of the total.

claim: "Thirty eight Excel files on a shared drive."
evidence: After fixing formats the register covers 38 properties, but as typed it holds 150 different property_code strings and 683 rows needed fixing. The merged-registers problem is visible.

claim: "We have RFC access for reading work orders, service entries and posting status."
evidence: The extract holds vendor_master (900 rows), work_orders (2,092), properties (38), posted_invoices (11,075) and the empty parsed_bill (0). None is a service-entry table, although the IT head says service entries can be read over RFC. Reading is approved; the extract is narrower than described.

claim: "If it is mandatory, they will." (use a portal)
evidence: Not testable. The survey puts portal preference at 9%.

claim: "Do not know where my bill is"
evidence: The data records dates, not what vendors were told.

claim: "Queries come late"
evidence: Queries are raised a mean of 22.2 days after the bill reaches the desk (median 20, never sooner than 7), and 10.2 days after head office receives it.

claim: "Same bill delivered to several places"
evidence: 136 bills (1.2%) share a vendor and invoice number with another bill, and 130 queries are raised as duplicates. Where a bill was delivered cannot be seen, so the survey's 33% of vendors cannot be compared.

claim: "Payment amount differs from bill without explanation"
evidence: The register has no paid-amount column.

claim: "MSME vendors registered as micro or small: payment within 45 days of accepting the goods or services, as required by law"
evidence: Same evidence as L5: the policy limit is breached for a share of bills that depends on which date starts the clock.

claim: "One of them is very senior, she has been here twelve years. She takes the big properties and anything complicated. The other four share the rest."
evidence: One verifier does carry the load: AP-1 handled 40.3% of bills (4,421), the other four 19.8%, 15.2%, 14.7% and 10.1%. But not by property: all 38 of 38 properties are served by all five verifiers, AP-1 is the main one at 38 of them (31.0% to 47.1% share), and the property mix and query rate are much the same (14.0% of AP-1's bills have a query against 11.1% to 14.3%). AP-1's bills wait 11.3 days for pick-up against 7.1 to 7.3 for the others. The data does not say AP-1 is the senior verifier.
